# Reflections on the Present

A mutual friend of ours—the retired sophomore, as we've come to call him—harbors a quiet concern about me. He worries that I will end up complacently fixated on future concerns, forever leaning toward what lies ahead rather than settling into the richness of the present moment. It's a fair worry, perhaps, and one I turn over in my mind more often than I'd admit.

Still, I find myself reflecting on how I appear "all right" in other people's dreams and perceptions. In their eyes, I seem steady, untroubled, whole—even as the ongoing business of living brings its steady stream of issues to consider, matters that never quite resolve themselves and never quite let me rest.

And so, even when I disagree with someone completely—when there isn't a single point on which we can find common ground—I still feel a deep and unexpected pride in them, a genuine fondness that refuses to be argued away. I want to encourage them. I want to tell them to celebrate, to feel good about who they are and what they've made of themselves. Disagreement, I've learned, need not cancel affection.

There are places I keep returning to, again and again. Some are real, some remembered, some perhaps only imagined: the Subfusc El Dorado, and those lost cities that, despite everything, still carry their old and familiar names. I go back to them the way one revisits an old song, finding comfort in their persistence.

So amid all the dismissive advice offered by others—and with the stormy weather already gathering on the horizon—I arrive at a simple conclusion. Life is ordinary. And in its very ordinariness, I find it satisfying enough.

# His And Feeling

There is something profound in the way we come to understand another person's inner world. His silence in the morning, his laughter at an unexpected joke, his hesitation before answering a difficult question—all of these are windows into a landscape we can never fully enter, yet forever try to reach.

**His** experiences shape everything about how he moves through the world. The choices he makes, the memories he carries, the hopes he tucks away for quieter moments—these belong to him alone, even as he shares them with those he trusts.

**And** in that small word lies the bridge between two people. It joins what might otherwise remain separate. His thoughts and hers. His past and his present. His fear and his courage. The word "and" refuses to let us choose only one thing; it insists that we can hold many truths at once. We are complicated, contradictory, and whole all at the same time.

**Feeling** is perhaps the hardest thing to translate into language. A feeling can arrive suddenly, like weather, and leave just as quickly. It can settle deep and stay for years. When he finally learns to name what he feels—the grief, the joy, the tangled mix of both—something shifts. Naming a feeling does not erase it, but it does make it possible to share.

Together, these three simple words remind us that every person is a story still being written. His journey, and the feelings that color it, deserve to be witnessed with patience and care.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, stream-of-consciousness prose poem full of non-sequiturs, mixing weather-report language with drinking toasts and cryptic life advice.
counterfactuals.output:
# Barometric Farewell, or How to Toast the Fog

Raise your glass to the low-pressure system moving in from wherever your mother kept the good scissors. *Salut* to the seventy percent chance of becoming someone you warned yourself about.

Here's to you.

The isobars are crowding like relatives at a will-reading, and I want you to know: never trust a man who folds his umbrella before the rain admits defeat. Cheers to that. Cheers to the dew point, which is just the sky learning to cry professionally.

*Skål.*

Winds out of the northeast at the speed of a decision you'll regret by Tuesday. A toast! A toast to Tuesday, that liar, that folded map, that drawer you keep meaning to fix. My grandfather said: *when the clouds come low, keep your knees soft and your promises softer.* Then he drank the porch light.

Prost. Prost to the front approaching. Prost to the front you present.

Scattered showers in the chest cavity, clearing by nightfall, unless the nightfall clears you first. Here's mud in your forecast. Here's to the migratory habits of everyone you loved in a hallway. The relative humidity is none of your business, but I'll tell you anyway—it's the exact amount required to make a photograph curl.

Bottoms up. The sky is a bottom. We are all up.

Advice, since you asked with your eyebrows: plant the tree you won't sit under, and water it with your least favorite excuse. Visibility is poor. Visibility has always been poor. That's why we invented the clinking sound, so we could find each other in the dark.

*L'chaim*, you gorgeous depression system.
*L'chaim*, you passing cold.

Frost advisory for the heart after midnight—bring the ferns inside, the ones you call feelings, the ones the cat keeps knocking off the sill. Gusts up to whatever your father never said. Here's to the barometer, that honest little coward, dropping and dropping and telling you nothing you can use.

So drink.

The weekend outlook is *maybe.* The weekend outlook is a hand on your shoulder that turns out to be a coat hook. Sunny with a chance of remembering. Overcast with a fifty-fifty shot at grace.

To the fog, then.

The fog doesn't care if you toast it. The fog is already inside your name, drinking your good stuff, folding your umbrella, telling your grandchildren *when the clouds come low—*

Cheers. Keep your knees soft.

Highs today. Lows forever. Partly you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental piece in the style of John Ashbery—disjointed, dreamlike, with sudden shifts between the mundane and the mysterious.
counterfactuals.output:
# Provisional Weather for the Undecided

The mail arrives, or doesn't. Either way
the geraniums have made up their minds
about the afternoon. You said something
about a train, but the train was already
a memory of itself, pulling into
a station that resembled your grandmother's kitchen
if the kitchen had been left out in the rain
of an idea we once had about happiness.

Meanwhile the philosophers are dining
on the shape of an argument. How pleasant.
The waiter brings a small cloud on a plate.
"Is this the one I ordered?" No one answers
because the question has drifted toward the window
where a boy is teaching a stone to whistle.

It's later than the clock is willing to admit.
We had been discussing the merits of a wall,
its firm opinion, when the wall dissolved
into a corridor of sighing violins,
or maybe it was just the refrigerator,
that patient beast, humming its one hymn.

And you, arriving in the tense you prefer,
the one that hasn't happened yet but aches—
you set your keys down on the table's edge
and all at once the whole room understood
something the room had always meant to say
but couldn't, being furniture, being *here*,
where the light does its slow forgetting
and the day, unfinished, folds itself away

like a letter no one will admit to writing,
addressed, in a hand we almost recognize,
to the person we were going to become
before the weather changed its provisional mind.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a monologue from an aging, philosophical narrator who rambles about mortality, lost cities, and pleasing himself, blending clichés with strange imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Cartographer of Nowhere**

Ah, sit—no, don't sit, you'll wear a groove in the chair, and grooves outlive us all, you know. Everything outlives us. The chair, the dust, the little moth that's been auditioning for immortality against my lamp for three nights running. *That* moth will outlast me, and it doesn't even pay rent.

Where was I? Mortality. Yes. They say time is a river. They *always* say time is a river, as if the man who first said it deserved a medal instead of a shrug. Time isn't a river, my friend—time is a landlord. It collects, it collects, it never fixes the plumbing, and one morning it changes the locks while you're still in your slippers.

I have seen lost cities. Or I have dreamed them, which at my age is the same accounting. There was one built entirely of the pauses between people's sentences—a whole metropolis of hesitation, its towers made of "well, you see" and its bridges of "I meant to call." I walked its avenues. I found nobody home, because nobody ever *finished* anything there. A beautiful place. Doomed, of course. Everything beautiful is doomed; that's how you can tell it apart from the furniture.

And another city, sunk beneath a sea the color of an old bruise, where the fish wore the faces of everyone I'd disappointed. They swam in schools, which is more education than most of them managed alive.

But do you know what I've learned, sitting here rotting agreeably like good fruit in a warm bowl? I've learned to please myself. Oh, don't smirk—I mean I've learned *contentment*, you filthy-minded amphibian. I mean I pour the tea and I *enjoy* the pouring. I let the honey drown slowly and I don't hurry it, because I have nowhere left to arrive. The great secret they don't tell you: when the future finally quits sending its invoices, the present becomes yours to squander. And I squander it magnificently. I spend whole hours watching that idiot moth.

They tell me I should make peace with the end. Make peace! As if death were a small country I'd been feuding with over a fence line. No—I've made something better than peace. I've made *acquaintance*. Death and I nod at each other in the hallway now, two old tenants who've stopped pretending we'll move out.

So. The river runs, the landlord counts, the cities sink, and the moth—look, look—the moth has finally touched the flame.

And it was pleased. For exactly one moment, it was so terribly, brilliantly pleased.

Aren't we all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write me an absurdist toast that sounds profound but doesn't quite make sense, ending with the line "Living is a meatloaf sandwich."
counterfactuals.output:
Raise your glasses, friends, and let us consider the unconsidered.

For too long we have chased the horizon, only to find it politely stepping backward, like a waiter who has forgotten our order but not our faces. We build our castles on the sand, yes—but who among us has asked the sand how it *feels* about the arrangement? Not I. Not you. Not the pelican.

They say time heals all wounds, but time is merely a clock that learned to walk, and a clock has no hands with which to bandage anything. We are all just passengers on a train that arrives before it departs, clutching tickets printed in a language we invented last Tuesday and have already forgotten.

Consider the moon. It does not strive. It simply *reflects*—and isn't that the truest form of ambition? To borrow one's light and never pay it back?

So tonight, let us not ask *why*. Let us not even ask *whether*. Let us instead lean gently into the great uncertain, hand in hand, unburdened by the weight of understanding, and remember the one truth that binds us all across the vast and buttered expanse of existence:

**Living is a meatloaf sandwich.**

*Cheers.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of avant-garde flash fiction where a speaker addresses a friend, drifts through half-formed memories and weather forecasts, and repeats "I do it in a lot of places."
counterfactuals.output:
The Weather in Places

Listen, Marguerite—no, you're not Marguerite, but let me call you that, the light is doing something to your face.

I do it in a lot of places.

There was rain expected Tuesday, or the Tuesday of some other year, the kind where you hold your coffee and don't drink it. My mother stood at a window like that. Or I did. The glass fogged from the inside, which means someone was breathing, which means someone was alive in the room, and forecasters call this a forty percent chance, this breathing.

You remember the ferry? You weren't there. I've decided you were there.

I do it in a lot of places—the deciding, I mean. I put people on boats they never boarded. I hang weather on days that stayed dry and cloudless and cruel.

High of sixty. Winds from the southwest. My father's hands, southwest, folding a map he couldn't read, saying *here, this is where we're going,* pointing at the ocean, at the blue part, at the part with no roads.

Are you cold? I'm always slightly—

I do it in a lot of places, the shivering. Grocery stores. That one museum. The wing with the broken clocks, all of them stopped at different wrongs.

You had a scarf once. Green. No. I'm building you again from parts. Forgive the seams.

Snow overnight, they said. Accumulation of one to three memories. Roads may be impassable, may be the roads I used to know, may be nothing, may be the smell of a house that burned down before I was born, that I remember anyway, that I insist on.

Friend—can I say friend?—the pressure is dropping.

I feel it in my knees, in the old places, the places that keep the weather even when the sky forgets.

I do it in a lot of places. I sit with someone almost like you and I talk toward the window and I let the forecast in and I mistake it for the past, or I mistake the past for something that could still be predicted, still be prepared for, still be survived with the right coat, the right—

Partly cloudly. Partly you. Partly the ferry we both weren't on.

Stay a little. The front's still moving through.

I do it in a lot of places, this asking.

This staying.

This is one of them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
